deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. It is a page of German lecture-style notes on ancient Hellenistic history: the succession to the Macedonian throne after the Galatian (Celtic) invasion. It continues p.180 (Lysimachus, Seleucus, Ptolemy Ceraunus, Sosthenes) and leads into p.182 (Achaean and Aetolian Leagues).

Content, paraphrased:
(1) The Gauls advanced as far as Delphi. When they stormed the temple an earthquake is said to have arisen, and Apollo drove them back by a miracle (279 BC, Brennus).
(2) Part of the Gauls settled in Thrace. Numerous bands went on to Asia Minor, where the kings of Bithynia ceded Galatia to them. The machine transcription's comma, 'Bithynien, Galatien', obscures this sense.
(3) After the Gauls withdrew there were two claimants to the throne: Antigonus 'of Gonni' (Gonatas), son of Demetrius Poliorcetes, and Antiochus (I Soter). Antigonus made a settlement and a marriage alliance with Antiochus (his marriage to Phila) and gained the throne.
(4) Pyrrhus, back from Italy in 274, invaded Macedonia and was acknowledged as king. Antigonus withdrew to the Peloponnese. Pyrrhus pursued him but was killed by an old woman (a roof tile at Argos) while trying to take the city, 272. Antigonus then recovered the throne and held it from then on.
(5) A genealogical tree of the Antigonid dynasty, with death years BC:
- Antigonus (I) †301
- Demetrius Poliorcetes †284
- Antigonus Gonatas †243
- then Demetrius II †233 and Antigonus Doson †221 as siblings
- under Demetrius II: Philip V †179
- under Philip V: Perseus †166 and Demetrius †180.

There is no derivation to reconstruct. The bundle label 'Lagrange1816' notwithstanding, this is history notes, possibly not even in Gauss's own hand (student or lecture notes).
errors: Antigonus Gonatas died 239 BC by modern chronology, not 243.
Demetrius II died 229 BC by modern chronology, not 233. Some older chronologies give earlier dates, so both this and the Gonatas date may reflect the source used.
Demetrius Poliorcetes is usually dated †283 BC; the note has 284.

The tree makes Antigonus Doson a sibling of Demetrius II under Gonatas. In fact Doson was the son of Demetrius the Fair, so he was Gonatas's nephew and Demetrius II's cousin. He ruled as guardian/regent for the young Philip V.
Numbering: Doson is conventionally Antigonus III, with Gonatas as Antigonus II. The label 'Antigonus II Doson', if read correctly, is off by one.

The narrative is otherwise consistent with standard accounts: Delphi 279, the Gauls' crossing to Asia Minor at Bithynian invitation, the Antigonus–Antiochus I peace and Phila marriage, Pyrrhus's return 275/274, and his death at Argos 272.

results.what: Narrative of the Galatian invasion, Antigonus Gonatas's accession, Pyrrhus's invasion and death, and an Antigonid genealogy
results.usually_credited_to: Standard ancient-history content (Justin, Plutarch, Pausanias; 18th–19th c. handbooks such as Heeren's)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is purely historical notes with no mathematical content. Such general-education notes in the Gauss papers are unremarkable, and the page may not even be in Gauss's hand.

checkable.asserts: Interval between the recorded death of Antigonus I (301) and that of Demetrius Poliorcetes (284) is 17 years.
Pyrrhus died 2 years after returning from Italy and invading Macedonia, per the notes.
The note's death year for Gonatas differs from the modern date (239 BC) by 4 years.

transcription_corrections: In the genealogy the names are written 'Demetrais poliorcetes' and 'Antigonus gannatas' (sic, i.e. Gonatas). The machine transcription normalizes these.
'Antiochus' after 'Demetrius poliorcetes und' carries a cross-like flourish in the image ('Antiochus†').
'wo ihnen die Könige von Bithynien, Galatien einräumten' should be read as 'the kings of Bithynia ceded Galatia to them'. The comma is not a list separator.
Doson's label in the tree appears as 'Antigonus II Doson' (with a double stroke). Philip appears as 'Philipp V'.
